content: 1. Day et al. (2016) discuss the implementation of a staff support program specifically designed for rural hospitals in Nepal, as published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 2. Goma FM and colleagues evaluate strategies for recruiting and retaining health workers in rural Zambia, highlighting the challenges and outcomes in their study published in Human Resources for Health. 3. Mkoka DA et al. explore the perspectives of health workers and managers on the factors influencing working conditions for maternal healthcare services in a rural district of Tanzania, emphasizing the sentiment that government employment often leads to neglect of staff needs. 4. Narayan V and colleagues investigate the impact of poor communication, job dissatisfaction, and attrition among rural health workers in Sierra Leone, as detailed in their study in Human Resources for Health. 5. Mays DC et al. assess the effectiveness of community health worker programs in supporting and retaining village health teams in two districts of Uganda, as published in the International Journal for Equity in Health. 6. Masango S and colleagues analyze the role of non-financial incentives in retaining health sector workers in Swaziland, as presented in the EQUINET Discussion Paper. 7. Belaid L et al. conduct a mixed-method study in Niger to understand the factors affecting the attraction and retention of health professionals in rural and remote areas, as published in Human Resources for Health. 8. Darkwa EK et al. perform a qualitative study on the factors influencing the retention of doctors and nurses in rural healthcare facilities in Bangladesh, as detailed in BMC Health Services Research. 9. Bilodeau H and Leduc N compile an inventory of the main factors determining the attraction, installation, and retention of physicians in remote areas, as published in Cahiers de Sociologie et de Démographie Médicales. 10. Glazebrook RM and Harrison SL identify obstacles and propose solutions for maintaining advanced procedural skills among rural and remote medical practitioners in Australia, as published in Rural and Remote Health. 11. Mansoor GF et al. examine midwifery retention, coverage, and its impact on service utilization in Afghanistan, as detailed in the journal Midwifery. 12. Gardiner M et al. evaluate the effectiveness of cognitive behavioral coaching in improving the well-being and retention of rural general practitioners, as published in the Australian Journal of Rural Health. 13. Gyekye SA investigates workers' perceptions of workplace safety and job satisfaction, as detailed in the International Journal of Occupational Safety and Ergonomics. 14. Majid A et al. analyze the impact of safety and health on employee retention, as published in the Management and Administrative Sciences Review. 15. Rahman SM et al. identify factors affecting the recruitment and retention of community health workers in a newborn care intervention in Bangladesh, as detailed in Human Resources for Health. 16. Abbey M et al. explore factors related to the retention of community health workers in a trial on community-based management of fever in children under five in Ghana, as published in International Health. 17. Bhattacharyya K et al. examine how incentives and disincentives affect the motivation, retention, and sustainability of community health workers, as summarized in Web Annex H. 18. Olang’o CO et al. investigate staff attrition among community health workers in home-based care programs for people living with HIV and AIDS in western Kenya, as detailed in Health Policy. 19. Rickard G et al. assess an organizational intervention aimed at reducing occupational stress and turnover among hospital nurses in the Northern Territory, Australia, as published in Collegian. 20. Bonenberger M et al. study the effects of health worker motivation and job satisfaction on turnover intention in Ghana, as detailed in Human Resources for Health. 21. Watanabe M et al. explore the impact of information technology on the physician workforce and healthcare in isolated communities in Canada, as published in the Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare. 22. Gruen RL et al. review the role of specialist outreach clinics in primary care and rural hospital settings, as detailed in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 23. Gagnon M-P et al. conduct a qualitative case study on the effects of telehealth on medical human resource supply in remote regions, as published in BMC Health Services Research. 24. Gagnon M-P et al. identify the conditions for successfully implementing telehealth to support medical practice in rural and remote regions, as detailed in Implementation Science. 25. Mbemba GIC et al. evaluate the influence of a telehealth project on healthcare professional recruitment and retention in remote areas of Mali, as published in SAGE Open Medicine. 26. Komaromy M et al. introduce Project ECHO, a model for educating primary care providers about treating substance use disorders, as detailed in the journal Substance Abuse. 27. Bagayoko C-O et al. discuss the use of e-health as a mechanism to recruit and retain healthcare professionals in remote areas, drawing lessons from the EQUi-ResHuS project in Mali, as published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making. 28. Bervell B and Al-Samarraie H provide a comparative review of mobile health and electronic health utilization in sub-Saharan African countries, as detailed in Social Science and Medicine. 29. Ly BA et al. describe the individual and contextual determinants of telemedicine use, based on perceptions of Senegalese physicians and telemedicine project managers, as published in PLoS One. 30. Coma del Corral MJ et al. evaluate the utility of a thematic network in primary healthcare through a controlled interventional study in a rural area, as detailed in Human Resources for Health. 31. Butterworth K et al. conduct a qualitative study on the retention of general practitioners in rural Nepal, as published in the Australian Journal of Rural Health. 32. Connolly M et al. examine the impact of longitudinal rural medical student clerkships on clinical supervisors and hospitals, as detailed in the Australian Journal of Rural Health. 33. Manahan C and Lavoie JG review the factors influencing rural nurse retention, as published in the Online Journal of Rural Nursing and Health Care. 34. Levesque M et al. analyze physician perceptions of recruitment and retention factors in an area with a regional medical campus, as detailed in the Canadian Medical Education Journal. 35. Mangham LJ and Hanson K investigate the employment preferences of public sector nurses in Malawi, as published in Tropical Medicine and International Health. 36. Wibulpolprasert S and Pengpaibon P review four decades of integrated strategies to address the inequitable distribution of doctors in Thailand, as detailed in Human Resources for Health. 37. Gardiner M et al. assess the impact of support initiatives on retaining rural general practitioners, as published in the Australian Journal of Rural Health. 38. Willis-Shattuck M et al. conduct a systematic review on the motivation and retention of health workers in developing countries, as detailed in BMC Health Services Research.
